label: paragraph_title
text: GROPING ITS WAY.

label: paragraph_title
text: "GOVERNMENT AND GENERAL STRIKE"

label: text
text: EMERGENCY PROSECUTION

label: text
text: Peaceful Picketing To Be Tolerated.

label: text
text: Both Sides are satisfied with the position in regard to the general strike at Home at the end of the second day.

label: text
text: A long struggle is being prepared for, and both the Trade Union Congress and the Government are marshalling all their forces.

label: text
text: A plea is still being urged by many for the resumption of the negotiations—so far without success.

label: text
text: HOUR TO HOUR POINTS.

label: text
text: "We are only at the beginning of an issue hitherto not experienced, and the Government is groping its way," emphasised Lord Birkenhead in the House of Lords, which passed the continuance of the Emergency Powers Act without a decision. Peaceful picketing will not at present be interfered with.

label: text
text: The Government is not prepared to negotiate as long as the threat "off a general strike holds the field.

label: text
text: Regular though attenuated train services, long distance and suburban are being maintained. The tubes are partially working. Buses are being marred by volunteers.

label: paragraph_title
text: PRICE, $3.00 Per Month.

label: text
text: A special strike edition of the Daily Herald was stopped by the police, who seized all the copies already printed.

label: text
text:
Up to yesterday 12,450 volunteers
workers had been enrolled.

label: text
text: Workers had been enrolled. The Trades Union Congress is confident of securing an honourable settlement.

label: text
text: Disorders have occurred through brumears and buses being attacked in England and Scotland. As a counter blast to the British Gazette the Trade Unions Congress is to publish a paper called the British Worker.

label: text
text: The Government notifies printers of its insistence in any settlement of a clause preventing victimisation of those who are doing their duty to the country. The official view of the whole position last night was very reassuring.

label: text
text: Fails between Ireland and Britain are suspended. Shilings between Holyhead and Dublin have been cancelled.

label: text
text: The effect of the strike on cricket and racing is reported on our Sports Page.

label: text
text: On the Cabinet heavy losses by growers of new potatoes and fruits intended for export to Great Britain are feared.

label: text
text: A strike of motor car factory workers is reported in sympathy with the British strikers. The American Press describes the strike as a tragedy, but ridicules any idea of a Revolution.

label: text
text: lengthy debate was opened on the emergency regulations. There was no personal rancour, all being anxious to assist in the search for a solution.

label: text
text: Mr. A. Henderson created a stir by referring to a formula which the Labourites had prepared to present to the Prime Minister when the negotiations were broken off.

label: paragraph_title
text: DEBATE IN LORDS.

label: paragraph_title
text: Not the Last of Government's Demands:

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: The fact that we are only at the beginning of an issue hitherto not experienced and that the Government is groping its way was em-

label: text
text:
phased by Lord Birkenhead in the House of Lords in supporting a motion to continue the Emergency Powers Act, which was carried without a division.
He declared that the Government at present did not intend to interfere "with peaceful picketing but was unable to give an assurance that this would be the list of the demands that the Government would have to make on Parliament.

label: text
text: He reiterated that the Government was not prepared to negotiate so long as the threat of a general strike held the field.

label: text
text: Tyrannical Power

label: text
text: Lord Buckmaster, in supporting the motion on behalf of the Liberals, spoke of one of the most

label: vision_footnote
text: LORD/ BURGERS MASTER

label: text
text: wanton exercises of tyrannical power the country had been called on to meet for centuries.

label: text
text: The debate produces a dialogue between Lord Haldane and Lord Birkenhead, when the latter demanded a clear and unequivocal statement as to whether Lord Haldane approved of the general strike.

label: text
text: The burden of Lord Haldane's contributions was that the negotiations ought to be continued.

label: paragraph_title
text: CONDITIONS DIFFERENT.

label: text
text: Second Day's Impressions in London.

label: text
text: Although it was the second day of the strike all the roads to the city were crowded with traffic, chiefly an endless procession of private cars and food lorries, yet the conditions were most different. A twelve mile run yesterday took two hours and to-day one hour.

label: text
text: A number of omnibuses are working on the principal routes, including the London and General, besides independent buses manned by volunteers, even the stairways of these being packed.

label: text
text: There were distinct evidences of regular, although attenuated, train services, both long distance and suburban.

label: text
text: The tubes are partially working. Queues are waiting outside the stations, which yesterday were closed.

label: text
text:
People coming to the City by long routes from the suburbs are most good-humoured in spite of the very dismal weather, drizzle, and mist.
A novel feature is the posting in windows of broadcast news bulletins, which are surrounded by eager crowds.

label: paragraph_title
text: NEWSPAPER SEIZED.

label: text
text: Police Raid on "Daily Herald" Offices.

label: text
text: A cordón of police surrounded the "Daily Herald" offices whilst a special strike edition was being printed.

label: text
text: They stopped the machines and seized all the papers so far printed, which were removed to Scotland Yard.

text: COST OF LIVING

label: text
text: If a Revolution is in progress in Great Britain it is being carried so far with the traditional British phlegm, the most striking outward evidence of which has been the amazing manifestation in the OFFICIAL STATISTICS.

label: paragraph_title
text: HOME MAILS

label: text
text: Arriving early at the G.P.O., this morning, delivery of the mail b the s.s. "Empress of Canada" commenced in the forenoon.

label: text
text: The mail comprised 354 bags from the U.S.A. and other countries, included in which were three bags letters and seven bags newspapers from London and seven bags from the continent, despatched via Siberia, also eight bags from the United Kingdom via Canada.

label: text
text: enormous increase of motor traffic as compared with the last industrial upheaval, the enirming earlier rising of people's anxious to reach business in the city by motor or afoot, and the unusually crowded ten shops supplying breakfasts.

label: text
text: There is an increase in the prices of certain food commodities, notably fish, which has doubled, and milk, which is 25 per cent. dearer to-day.

label: paragraph_title
text: Both Sides Satisfied

label: text
text: Both sides are satisfied with the position.

label: text
text: The Government Spokesman today broadcast that the position throughout the country was satisfactory. There was no sign of panic or even of great excitement, and no serious disturbance anywhere. Food supplies were normal, and 12,450 volunteers had so far been enrolled in London. Volunteers are flowing in all over the country.

label: text
text: An announcement is made by the Trade Unions Congress that the response of the workers to the strike call has surpassed expectations. The difficulty of the General Council has been to keep men at work in trades which are “the second line of defence.” Everywhere there is order and good temper. The Council is confident of securing an honourable settlement.

label: paragraph_title
text: PRESS OUTLOOK.

label: paragraph_title
text: Labour's Official Organ.

label: text
text: Apart from an attenuated Times, the "British Gazette," the financial papers, and the "Daily Mirror," the last of which succeeded in distributing in London, and the news bulletin, whose five-line leading article exhorted its readers to stand fast in support of the Government, no papers are published in London to-day.

label: text
text: The Trades Union Council announces its intention of responding to the Government's "British Gazette" by publishing from the "Daily Herald" office a newspaper called the "British Worker".

label: text
text: A characteristic of the British touch of "Revolution" is the delivery of piles of telegrams to the Trades Union Congress headquarter in London by Government employees, also the American maila being conveyed in motors from Southampton by volunteers, whom the Trades Union Congress designate as blacklegs, and also the Government telephones working normally at the Labour Bureaus. It is noteworthy that the strikers cut off the "Daily Mirror" from the Telephone Exchange and persuaded the cleaning staff to leave the building in retaliation for the publication of the news bulletin.

label: paragraph_title
text: LADY'S INJURIES.

label: paragraph_title
text: KOWLOON LADY CLAIMS

label: text
text: PINNED DOWN BY BUS.

label: text
text: Arising out of a Kowloon bus incident, Mrs. H. A. Jones was the plaintiff in a Summary Court case this morning (before the Puisna Judge, Mr. Justice J. R. Wood) when the Kal Tack Motor Bus Co., Ltd. were sued for $1,000 special and general damages for injuries alleged to have been caused by negligence of the part of the company's servants.

label: text
text:
Evidence had not completed when the Court rose for tiffin.
Mr. T. J. Andrews was for Mrs. Jones and Mr. D. L. Strellett defended

label: text
text:
Jones and Mr. D. L. Strellett defended.
Medical evidence of the extent of the injuries sustained by Mrs. Jones was given by Dr. M. Nicholson and Dr. W. Leslie Thomas, Dr. Nicholson stating that the injuries had every appearance of being caused by a direct blow. Ulcers had appeared as a result of the tissues being destroyed. Weakness of the muscles of the leg was still in evidence and necessitated the use of a stick and of an elastic bandage. Mrs. Jones would probably eventually recover the normal use of the limb but it would take a considerable time. He had had to be consulted up to the present, on no less than sixteen occasions. On his advice the services of a masse use had also been secured.

label: text
text: Mr. Strellet asked witness if he had been present when an examination was made by Dr. MacGown and witness said he had but His Honour disallowed further questions on this point as the evidence of Dr. MacGown was not to be called.

label: text
text: Mrs. Jones was accorded a sent in the witness-box. The effect of her evidence was that on January 27, between 11 and 11:30 a.m., she was returning home, with her aunt (who had since left for Australia), by a Kai Tack bus, from Kowloon City, having come from the Kowloon golf course.

label: text
text: The bus was going very quickly. Near Bailey's yard, the driver seemed to lose control and swerved to the right, falling over on its left side. She was pinned to the ground with the bus over her legs.

label: text
text: I think the driver was half asleep," added Mrs. Jones who also spoke about the left rear wheel coming off. She was at the left end of the front row of seats. The bus, which was "very old," was full.

label: text
text: In cross-examination, Mrs. Jones stated that the bus fell quickly; she did not have time to step down and save herself. "I hung on to the bar or I would have been killed," she said.

label: text
text:
Her husband had owned a car for years and she considered herself to be a judge of speed.
An Indian constable who was on duty at the spot...at the time, said he saw the bus going very fast. He turned to take its number and the bus fell over as he was about to do so. He was not sure as to whether the wheel came off first, or not.

label: paragraph_title
text: SEVERAL INCIDENTS REPORTED

label: text
text: EUROPEANS' LOSSES.

label: text
text: Several cases of theft are disclosed in reports made to the police yesterday.

label: text
text: Sergeant Major Edwards of the Royal Engineers, while at Victoria Barracks left his coat on a table in the office of the Survey Department. A sum of $140 in bank notes was stolen from the pocket.

label: text
text: Mrs. R. Miller, of No. 3, Mody Road, Kowloon, lost a sum of $400 in bank notes from a locked drawer in her dressing room. The theft was committed between Tuesday afternoon and yesterday.

label: text
text: The house of a Chinese forman of the Kowloon-Canton Railway at Shatin was entered on Monday night by three men, one of whom carried a torch. Access was gained by the front door which was closed but not locked. Runsucking the house they took a small quantity of money and clothing.

label: text
text: A Singer sewing machine valued at $100 is reported to have been stolen from a tailor's shop at UnLong.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: NOTABLE ISSUE

label: text
text:
Na, 1, of volume 5, of the “Silver Wolf,” is out. It is the official organ of the Boy Scouts Association of Hongkong.
Mr. C. H. Blason is the editor; and Messrs. M. J. Baptista, E. L. Sim and A. Kirk are the art editors. Officials of the Association, of twenty local troops and five Wolf Cub packs are given together with a list of members.

label: text
text: There is some very interesting, and highly instructive reading matter in the magazine. Attaining to exemplary, ideals, the "Silver Wolf"—like its predecesors—has much to tell the layman and those not yet acquainted with scouting.

label: text
text: Items of particular note are: The Commissioner's letter; camping notes; what to do in case of fire; competition details and results; "jottings"; A message to Scouts and Girl Guides from the Chief Scout; A trip to Hangchow; troop notes; and notes for Cubs; Rovers and Scouters.
